item.title: Mao Zedong and China's Cultural Revolution (3/3) | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
From peasants' son to revolutionary leader — Mao Zedong laid the foundation for modern China. This three-part documentary offers an in-depth look at one of the most influential figures of the 20th century.
The legacy of the "founding father" of the People's Republic of China remains deeply controversial. Revered in Europe as a revolutionary icon in the late 1960s, Mao led China to the brink of disaster and ultimately clung to power with a regime of terror. Yet today's leaders in Beijing continue to draw on the cult of Mao. China is now a global power, a transformation that would be difficult to imagine without Mao Zedong.
When Mao Zedong was born in 1893, nothing hinted at his meteoric rise to power. The son of a farming family, he grew up during a period of political instability and profound social upheaval. The 1911 Revolution, which marked the beginning of the end of imperial rule, awakened his mind to politics. At first, Mao had no clear political program. But the Russian Revolution of 1917 introduced him to Marxist ideas, and he soon became a co-founder of the Communist Party of China.
Mao rose steadily through the party ranks as conflict with the nationalist Kuomintang party intensified into a bloody civil war. The devastating retreat that became known as the "Long March" went down in history to become the foundation of the cult of Mao. After World War II, the struggle for power in China continued until Mao and his forces finally reached Beijing.
This three-part series traces Mao Zedong's journey from peasants' son to revolutionary and architect of modern China — from his rural childhood to the founding of the People's Republic to the devastating impact of the Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, which claimed millions of lives.
Archival footage, as well as interviews with historians and eyewitnesses, tell the story of the man who changed China forever.

item.title: Matisse: The Red Studio: Great Art Explained
item.author: Great Art Explained
item.content:encoded:
My book Great Art Explained is ready to order now worldwide US - https://a.co/d/52C1D6c UK - https://amzn.eu/d/6EoTxjs Spain - https://www.fnac.pt/Obras-maestras-ex... Also available in many other countries Latin and Central America India now, China and Korea soon My new Podcast can be found here! https://lnk.bio/primoandpayne
Today Henri Matisse’s the red studio is considered one of the landmarks of modern art, seen by thousands of visitors at the Museum of Modern art in New York. But before arriving there in 1948 it spent more than a decade hanging in a London nightclub.
When Matisse painted the red studio in 1911 it was one of the strangest pictures anyone had ever seen - a room almost completely consumed by red – furniture reduced to outlines, paintings hanging on walls that barely seem to exist, and a grandfather clock with 12 numbers but no hands. Even Matisse wasn't entirely sure what he had created and nobody wanted to buy it.
So how did a painting that even its creator struggle to understand, go from rejection and obscurity to becoming a masterpiece of modern art and what was it doing in a London nightclub in the first place?

item.title: How students took climate justice to the world's top court | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
In 2019, a group of 27 law students from the Pacific Islands launched a campaign to bring climate justice to the world's highest court, calling on wealthy countries to take greater responsibility for climate change.
Normally, only states or recognized organizations can submit cases to the International Court of Justice. But the students wanted people directly affected by climate change to have a voice.
Wealthy industrialized countries largely opposed these calls, arguing that international climate law does not clearly hold countries responsible for past emissions.

item.author: Patrick Boyle

Go to http://ground.news/pb for a better way to stay informed. Subscribe for 40% off unlimited access to worldwide coverage through my link.
In October 2026, Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out three of Yandex’s six major data centers, and a viral chart claimed that Russian bots had vanished from social media overnight. They hadn’t. In this video, we look at what the strikes actually hit: Yandex’s search crawlers, Russia’s taxi and payment apps, and the apartment gates of Moscow. We also look at why Russia’s data localization law left so much of its internet within drone range. Then we follow the real infrastructure of online influence operations, from residential proxy botnets and SIM farms to the off-brand 55-dollar Android TV boxes that rent out their owners’ internet connections. Along the way, we cover state-backed disinformation campaigns from Russia, China, Iran, and the West; the Sri Lankan academies teaching rage bait for Facebook ad revenue; the “supersharers” behind most fake news on Twitter; and new research from Anthropic on self-replicating AI that could run on the same cheap devices.

item.title: The housing crisis in Los Angeles - Between homelessness and luxury real estate | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles' housing crisis is escalating dramatically. Those who can't find a place to live have to get creative — otherwise, survival becomes a daily struggle.
Even before the devastating fires of January 2025, affordable housing was in short supply in Los Angeles. Even people earning an average full-time salary are at risk of ending up on the streets. In 2024, the number of homeless people in Los Angeles County was well over 75,000. The chronic housing shortage is driving residents to get creative, while also giving rise to new business ideas: Gregory sells camper vans to working people who can't afford to rent an apartment. He came up with the idea after he himself had to live in a camper van for a while. Car mechanic Roy also lives in a mobile home. The 64-year-old has to supplement his modest pension by working at an auto repair shop.
Since 2012, Elvina, who immigrated to the US, has been renting out beds in large communal dorms for 55 dollars a night. It's a popular solution, and many long-term residents enjoy the social atmosphere. Elvina now operates seven of these facilities throughout California. Meanwhile Shelton, a real estate agent, is living a picture-perfect American dream. She sells luxury homes and lives with her husband and children in the upscale Brentwood neighborhood. It took more than just hard work to achieve her success: the 42-year-old also had to overcome her alcohol addiction. James has now made it off the streets after living for a time in the notorious Skid Row district in the heart of downtown L.A. He wants to give something back, so once a week he offers free haircuts to those who need them. This documentary looks at varying lifestyles and living conditions in a city where the gap between rich and poor is growing ever wider.

item.title: The WILD Medieval History Of Eleanor of Aquitaine
item.author: History Hit
item.content:encoded:
Eleanor of Aquitaine was one of the most powerful figures of the medieval world: twice a queen, a crusader, a rebel and the architect of an empire.
Through her marriages to Louis VII of France and Henry II of England, she helped create the vast Angevin Empire and reshape European politics. She led forces on the Second Crusade, rebelled against her husband and played a decisive role in the rise of her sons, including Richard the Lionheart and King John.
Historian Dr Elena Janega, host of Gone Medieval, joins the podcast to explore Eleanor’s extraordinary life - from the vibrant court of Aquitaine and the failure of the Second Crusade, to her dramatic divorce, imprisonment, and enduring political influence. This episode reveals how Eleanor’s authority and intelligence held a volatile dynasty together until her death.

item.title: Your location isn’t private | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Why do data brokers have your location data? And what do they use it for?
One big reason is advertising. Data brokers collect location data from people around the world and sell it to advertising companies who use it to create highly targeted ads.
This data comes from everyday apps on your phone, like maps, games, dating apps, and weather apps. The apps often collect this information to improve their services, but it can also end up in a global network of data brokers.
One main issue is that this data can be extremely detailed, showing where people live, work, and spend their free time. With this information, discerning a person's identity can be surprisingly easy, which can pose a serious security risk.
Although the trade in location data is regulated in certain places, like the EU, advertising companies and data brokers still find ways to access and use citizens' personal data.

item.title: The Global North taken to court - Who pays for the climate catastrophe? | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
From their lecture halls to the International Court of Justice. Law students from the South Pacific have joined island nations to demand greater climate accountability from industrialized countries.
The case before the world's highest court was initiated by 27 law students at the University of the South Pacific, all from islands that could become uninhabitable as sea levels rise and storms grow more frequent.
As might be expected, the Global North has pushed back against their demands for greater responsibility for the consequences of climate change. The United States and Germany argue that international climate law doesn't clearly make countries responsible for past emissions. The young law students are going up against opponents who know the international stage inside and out. What gives them the courage and determination to keep going?
In 2023 they achieved an early victory: their campaign for climate justice won the support of the U.N. General Assembly. That lead to a resolution calling for the international community to take action on climate change.
We follow Vishal from Fiji and Jule from Germany. Both are fighting for justice and compensation for climate-related damage in developing countries. Their journey takes them into the world of international diplomacy, where they confront powerful opponents — among them industrialized nations and oil companies who don't want to have to pay out billions in reparations. All the while, lobbyists and diplomats from major nations try to sway the voices of small island states.
The film captures the optimism of these young people who, full of determination and hope, demand accountability on behalf of the generations to come. Exclusive interviews with judges and historical footage highlight the importance of the case. In July 2025, it all culminates in an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice.

item.title: How humans and fridges stay cool
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
Why does sweating cool you down? When sweat evaporates, it carries heat away with it. Your fridge works the same way. A refrigerant inside turns from liquid to gas, pulling the warmth out of your food and releasing it into your kitchen.

item.title: U.S. Voters Share Their Views & Lives | American Voices 2026 (full documentary)| FRONTLINE (PBS)
item.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
item.content:encoded:
Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, how are voters FRONTLINE has been following since 2020 feeling about the direction of the country?
This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb
And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate
Over the past six years, a team of filmmakers has been following more than a dozen Americans — from a doctor to a pastor to a barber to a construction company owner to a retiree — in eight states across the U.S.
A month before the midterms, how are these Americans feeling about changes in the country and in their own lives?
Their diverse views and experiences unfold in “American Voices 2026,” a 90-minute FRONTLINE documentary that offers a meaningful look at both what unites and divides the U.S. electorate as the midterms approach.
From a team led by award-winning filmmaker Mike Shum, “American Voices 2026” is the latest installment of a unique filmmaking effort begun in 2020. That’s when Shum and FRONTLINE started documenting the lives of voters with differing viewpoints as they navigated a year of extraordinary tumult, from the pandemic to protests to the polls, in the documentary “American Voices: A Nation in Turmoil.” Four years later, “American Voices 2024” chronicled how their hopes and fears had changed since 2020.
Now, “American Voices 2026” explores how their perspectives have evolved amid another polarizing election season, a faltering economy, and a war with Iran that’s now in its eighth month.
Filmed in locations ranging from the Austin, Texas area, to Hayward, California; from Minneapolis, Minnesota, to Beaverdam, Virginia; and from Portland, Oregon, to Sioux City, Iowa, “American Voices 2026” is a journey across geography, race and politics that illuminates where our country has been — and where it is headed.

item.title: Inside RFK's Assassination: Minute-By-Minute
item.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
item.content:encoded:
Eight shots in a crowded kitchen corridor. A fallen frontrunner. And questions that never faded.
On June 5, 1968, Robert F. Kennedy was shot at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles moments after a primary-night speech. This episode traces the path to that midnight chaos: RFK’s war on Jimmy Hoffa and the Mafia, clashes with J. Edgar Hoover, his civil rights crusade, and a Portland synagogue speech urging stronger US support for Israel that sparked fierce backlash. Inside the pantry, we revisit Sirhan Sirhan’s .22 revolver, the eyewitness confusion, and the forensic riddle of a fatal shot behind the left ear. Why did the official record remain so thin? What fueled rumors of a second gunman? And how did a trial, a commuted sentence, and years of denied parole leave lingering doubts?
Watch to follow the timeline, hear the key voices, and explore the evidence that still divides historians and investigators without giving away the conclusions. Stay to decide for yourself.
